1	In the money or out of the money?
     2	 The buyer ("owner") of an option has the right, but not the obligation, to exercise the option on
     3	or before expiration. A call option5 gives the owner the right to buy the underlying security; a put
     4	option6 gives the owner the right to sell the underlying security.
     5	
     6	
     7	 Conversely, when you sell an option, you may be assigned—at any time regardless of the ITM
     8	amount—if the option owner chooses to exercise. The option seller has no control over assignment and
     9	no certainty as to when it could happen. Once the assignment notice is delivered, it's too late to
    10	close the position and the option seller must fulfill the terms of the options contract:
    11	
    12	
    13	 A long call exercise results in buying the underlying stock at the strike price.
    14	 A short call assignment results in selling the underlying stock at the strike price.
    15	 A long put exercise results in selling the underlying stock at the strike price.
    16	 A short put assignment results in buying the underlying stock at the strike price.
    17	 An option will likely be exercised if it's in the option owner's best interest to do so, meaning
    18	it's optimal to take or to close a position in the underlying security at the strike price rather
    19	than at the current market price. After the market close on expiration day, ITM options may be
    20	automatically exercised, whereas OTM options are not and typically expire worthless (often referred
    21	to as being "abandoned"). The table below spells it out.
    22	
    23	
    24	 If the underlying stock price is...
    25	 ...higher than the strike price
    26	 ...lower than the strike price
    27	 If the underlying stock price is...
    28	 A long call is...
    29	 ...higher than the strike price
    30	 ...ITM and typically exercised
    31	 ...lower than the strike price
    32	 ...OTM and typically abandoned
    33	 If the underlying stock price is...
    34	 A short call is...
    35	 ...higher than the strike price
    36	 ...ITM and typically assigned
    37	 ...lower than the strike price
    38	 ...OTM and typically abandoned
    39	 If the underlying stock price is...
    40	 A long put is...
    41	 ...higher than the strike price
    42	 ...OTM and typically abandoned
    43	 ...lower than the strike price
    44	 ...ITM and typically exercised
    45	 If the underlying stock price is...
    46	 A short put is...
    47	 ...higher than the strike price
    48	 ...OTM and typically abandoned
    49	 ...lower than the strike price
    50	 ...ITM and typically assigned
    51	 The guidelines in the table assume a position is held all the way through expiration. Of course,
    52	you typically don't need to do that. And in many cases, the usual strategy is to close out a
    53	position ahead of the expiration date. We'll revisit the close-or-hold decision in the next section
    54	and look at ways to do that. But assuming you do carry the options position until the end, there are
    55	a few things you need to consider:
    56	
    57	
    58	 Know your specs. Each standard equity options contract controls 100 shares of the underlying stock.
    59	That's pretty straightforward. Non-standard options may have different deliverables. Non-standard
    60	options can represent a different number of shares, shares of more than one company stock, or
    61	underlying shares and cash. Other products—such as index options or options on futures—have
    62	different contract specs.
    63	 Stock and options positions will match and close. Suppose you're long 300 shares of XYZ and short
    64	one ITM call that's assigned. Because the call is deliverable into 100 shares, you'll be left with
    65	200 shares of XYZ if the option is assigned, plus the cash from selling 100 shares at the strike
    66	price.
    67	 It's automatic, for the most part. If an option is ITM by as little as $0.01 at expiration, it will
    68	automatically be exercised for the buyer and assigned to a seller. However, there's something called
    69	a do not exercise (DNE) request that a long option holder can submit if they want to abandon an
    70	option. In such a case, it's possible that a short ITM position might not be assigned. For more, see
    71	the note below on pin risk7?
    72	 You'd better have enough cash. If an option on XYZ is exercised or assigned and you are "uncovered"
    73	(you don't have an existing long or short position in the underlying security), a long or short
    74	position in the underlying stock will replace the options. A long call or short put will result in a
    75	long position in XYZ; a short call or long put will result in a short position in XYZ. For long
    76	stock positions, you need to have enough cash to cover the purchase or else you'll be issued a
    77	margin8 call, which you must meet by adding funds to your account. But that timeline may be short,
    78	and the broker, at its discretion, has the right to liquidate positions in your account to meet a
    79	margin call9. If exercise or assignment involves taking a short stock position, you need a margin
    80	account and sufficient funds in the account to cover the margin requirement.
    81	 Short equity positions are risky business. An uncovered short call or long put, if assigned or
    82	exercised, will result in a short stock position. If you're short a stock, you have potentially
    83	unlimited risk because there's theoretically no limit to the potential price increase of the
    84	underlying stock. There's also no guarantee the brokerage firm can continue to maintain that short
    85	position for an unlimited time period. So, if you're a newbie, it's generally inadvisable to carry
    86	an options position into expiration if there's a chance you might end up with a short stock
    87	position.
    88	 A note on pin risk: It's not common, but occasionally a stock settles right on a strike price at
    89	expiration. So, if you were short the 105-strike calls and XYZ settled at exactly $105, there would
    90	be no automatic assignment, but depending on the actions taken by the option holder, you may or may
    91	not be assigned—and you may not be able to trade out of any unwanted positions until the next
    92	business day.
    93	
    94	
    95	 But it goes beyond the exact price issue. What if an option is ITM as of the market close, but news
    96	comes out after the close (but before the exercise decision deadline) that sends the stock price up
    97	or down through the strike price? Remember: The owner of the option could submit a DNE request.
    98	
    99	
   100	 The uncertainty and potential exposure when a stock price and the strike price are the same at
   101	expiration is called pin risk. The best way to avoid it is to close the position before expiration.
   102	
   103	
   104	 The decision tree: How to approach expiration
   105	 As expiration approaches, you have three choices. Depending on the circumstances—and your
   106	objectives and risk tolerance—any of these might be the best decision for you.
   107	
   108	
   109	 1. Let the chips fall where they may. Some positions may not require as much maintenance. An
   110	options position that's deeply OTM will likely go away on its own, but occasionally an option that's
   111	been left for dead springs back to life. If it's a long option, the unexpected turn of events might
   112	feel like a windfall; if it's a short option that could've been closed out for a penny or two, you
   113	might be kicking yourself for not doing so.
   114	
   115	
   116	 2. Close it out. If you've met your objectives for a trade, then it might be time to close it out.
   117	Otherwise, you might be exposed to risks that aren't commensurate with any added return potential

Based solely on `doc.txt`, here is what the document does and does not support about your plan:

**The document never discusses credit spreads.** The article, "In the money or out of the money?", covers only single long and short option positions. It contains no mention of put credit spreads, multi-leg strategies, or the concept of "defined risk" for any strategy. Therefore, the document gives you no basis to conclude that a put credit spread would have defined risk. The only risk characterization it offers is that an uncovered short call or long put, if assigned or exercised, results in a short stock position with "potentially unlimited risk" — but that statement is about short *stock* positions, not about spreads.

**On assignment, the document is direct and unfavorable to your goal of avoiding shares.** It states that when you sell an option, "you may be assigned—at any time regardless of the ITM amount—if the option owner chooses to exercise. The option seller has no control over assignment and no certainty as to when it could happen. Once the assignment notice is delivered, it's too late to close the position."

For short puts specifically, the document says: "A short put assignment results in buying the underlying stock at the strike price." Its table confirms that if the underlying stock price is lower than the strike price, a short put is ITM and "typically assigned," while if the stock is higher than the strike, it is OTM and "typically abandoned." It adds that if an option is ITM by as little as $0.01 at expiration, it is automatically exercised for the buyer and assigned to the seller, unless the holder submits a do-not-exercise (DNE) request.

**Crucially, the document describes exactly the outcome you want to avoid.** It explains: "If an option on XYZ is exercised or assigned and you are 'uncovered' (you don't have an existing long or short position in the underlying security), a long or short position in the underlying stock will replace the options. A long call or short put will result in a long position in XYZ." In other words, a short put that gets assigned converts into a long stock position — you would own the shares. The document also warns that for long stock positions you need enough cash to cover the purchase or you'll face a margin call, which the broker can meet by liquidating positions in your account.

**The document does not say that adding a long put leg (the spread) prevents this.** Because it never addresses spreads, it cannot confirm that the spread structure caps your loss or that you would be spared from receiving shares if the short put leg is assigned. All it tells you is that a short put, when assigned, results in buying the underlying at the strike.

**One additional caveat the document raises is pin risk:** if a stock settles exactly on a strike at expiration, there is no automatic assignment, but "depending on the actions taken by the option holder, you may or may not be assigned—and you may not be able to trade out of any unwanted positions until the next business day." The document's recommended way to avoid this uncertainty is to close the position before expiration.

**Bottom line:** Based only on this document, I cannot confirm that a put credit spread would have defined risk, because the document does not discuss credit spreads at all. And regarding your desire not to own Apple stock, the document explicitly states that a short put assignment results in buying the underlying stock at the strike price, and that sellers have no control over whether or when assignment occurs. The document provides no assurance that a spread would prevent you from being assigned shares.
